lesson.title: Cloud-native and disaggregated DBMSs: locality becomes a protocol
lesson.short: Compute/storage separation · ownership · logging · failure recovery
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Separating resources makes scaling more flexible. It also moves familiar memory and recovery decisions across a network.
goals: Compare shared-nothing, shared-storage and compute-memory-storage designs.
Trace page ownership, write-ahead logging and recovery responsibilities.
Estimate remote-access costs and design a workload/failure experiment.

sections.title: How to use this supplemental session
sections.html: This is an original supplemental study session aligned to the user-provided syllabus. It is not an Edinburgh lecture or a verified Canvas assignment. The Canvas reading list and instructor-specific assessment instructions were not accessible. Suggested activities, timings, templates and checks below are practice guidance, not official requirements.

sections.title: Draw the resource and responsibility boundaries
sections.html:
In a shared-nothing design, each worker owns a partition with its compute and local resources; cross-partition work needs communication. In compute-storage separation, multiple compute nodes access a durable storage service. A further memory layer can provide shared buffers or coordination independently of compute. CXL memory expansion and RDMA-accessed remote memory are different mechanisms; a network diagram alone does not specify either one.

Disaggregation can make resource scaling and pooling more flexible, but a new compute node may start with a cold cache. Reads may traverse a network; metadata and lock ownership may move; the control plane must route requests and track membership. “Serverless” describes an operational abstraction, not the absence of servers, failure modes or cost.

For every box in the design, write down its owned state, durability, replication, consistency and failure behavior. Distinguish a compute cache from an authoritative page version and from durable log storage.

Key takeaway

Independent scaling does not imply independent correctness. Coordination and durability contracts still connect the layers.

sections.title: Worked example: latency, bandwidth and caching
sections.html:
Original model. A query needs 1,000 remote 8 KiB pages. At an assumed usable bandwidth of 2 GiB/s, transferring 8,192,000 bytes takes about 3.81 ms. If each page also incurs a serialized 0.2 ms round trip, latency alone is 200 ms. These are simplified components, not a performance prediction; requests can overlap, bandwidth can be shared and queues can dominate.

With 100 outstanding requests, an idealized latency lower bound is roughly 10 rounds×0.2 ms=2 ms, while the bandwidth component remains 3.81 ms. Depending on overlap, total time is not simply their sum; a lower bound is at least the larger component before other work. Reducing dependency chains can matter more than reducing bytes.

A warm cache with a 90% hit ratio cuts remote pages to 100 in this toy model. A scale-out experiment that compares a warm old node with a cold new node confounds architecture with cache state. Report warm-up policy and both steady-state and scale-transition behavior.

Exercise: a query saves 50% of its remote bytes but leaves a serial chain of 100 requests unchanged. Must its latency halve?

Worked answer. No. If request latency dominates, byte reduction has little effect on that serial chain. Measure dependency depth, concurrency, queueing, CPU work and transfer volume separately.

sections.title: Multi-primary writes and recovery
sections.html:
Shared storage does not automatically make simultaneous writers safe. Two compute nodes caching the same page need a coherent ownership or version protocol. A transaction must know whether its reads are valid, how it obtains write authority and when another node can observe its changes.

Original failure trace. Node A updates a cached page. Before acknowledging commit, the system must satisfy its durable-commit rule for the corresponding log/commit information. A then fails before the modified page reaches its final storage location. Recovery must reconstruct the committed change from durable evidence and fence stale owners. If A acknowledged a write that existed only in volatile private memory, losing A could lose an acknowledged transaction.

Independent logs need an ordering/dependency strategy where operations interact. Do not equate a locally increasing sequence number with a globally sufficient recovery order. Failover also needs a way to prevent a partitioned former owner from continuing to write as though it were current.

sections.title: Read two concrete multi-primary designs
sections.html:
PolarDB-MP (SIGMOD 2024 Industry) uses disaggregated memory and storage. Its PMFS service coordinates transaction visibility, buffers and locks, and the paper describes partial ordering of log records and recovery. It is a published industrial paper in the SIGMOD Companion, not a PODS or SIGMOD research-track paper. Read its contention and network assumptions alongside its measurements.

GaussDB (PVLDB 2024) separates compute, memory and storage, with global buffer/lock services and page ownership. Placement and query routing exploit affinity to reduce transfers; recovery combines memory/storage mechanisms. Compare where ownership lives and what moves under contention, rather than treating the two architectures as interchangeable.

As another implementation example, Neon’s official architecture account separates compute from WAL safekeepers and page-serving responsibilities. This historical design account is useful for tracing durability, not for inferring a current SLA, price or every implementation detail.

sections.title: Mini-experiment: isolate the benefit and the network cost
sections.html:
Suggested scoped experiment. Implement or configure a small page-cache/storage microbenchmark, or use an accessible research artifact. A controlled latency/bandwidth model on one machine can test a mechanism, but it is not a reproduction of RDMA, CXL or a production disaggregated database.

  1. Compare local access, remote access without caching, and remote access with the same fixed cache budget. Use sequential and random reads, then vary working-set size and skew.
  2. Report latency distribution, throughput, bytes transferred, cache hit rate, CPU utilization and request concurrency. Sweep round-trip delay separately from bandwidth.
  3. For a multi-writer prototype, vary hot-page contention and transaction locality. Count ownership transfers, aborts/retries and time spent coordinating.
  4. Test recovery in a disposable sandbox: crash compute after durable commit and before page flush; validate committed state and measure recovery time. A toy failure test is not a high-availability certification.
  5. Compare fixed-total-resource scale-out with scale-out that adds resources. Label both. A larger cluster cannot establish architectural efficiency without a cost/resource denominator.

This project mostly needs CPU, memory, storage and a suitable network. One or two H100s do not reproduce RDMA/CXL or production control-plane behavior. Prefer a narrow emulation claim over an unsupported cloud-system claim.

sections.title: Exercises and synthesis
sections.html:
Return to buffer management, concurrency control, WAL and distributed transactions from the core lessons. Disaggregation rearranges their costs and responsibilities; it does not remove their invariants.

Exercise: a new node doubles total cache capacity and throughput improves 1.6×. What else must be tested?

Worked answer. Separate the effect of added cache from the placement/coordination design. Compare equal total memory, disclose CPU/network differences, measure cold-start and steady-state behavior, and test a working set large enough to exceed the original cache.

Exercise: storage is replicated, so a compute failure needs no recovery protocol. Is that correct?

Worked answer. No. Replication must include the right durable information, and the system still needs commit status, coherent versions/ownership, replay rules and fencing. Replicated old pages alone may not represent the latest committed state.

Key takeaway

A useful cloud-native evaluation includes transitions and failures, not only steady-state peak throughput.

quiz.question: What does compute-storage disaggregation alone guarantee?
options: Linear scaling with compute nodes.
A separation of resource roles; other guarantees need explicit protocols.
No need for concurrency control.
Zero cold-start overhead.
quiz.explanation: Disaggregation is an architectural separation. Scalability, correctness, recovery and latency depend on mechanisms and workload.

questions.question: In a simplified remote-page model, what is a risk of issuing many dependent requests serially?
options: Bandwidth becomes infinite.
Latency accumulates even when total bytes are modest.
Caches can no longer exist.
All reads become writes.
questions.explanation: Serial dependency chains pay repeated request latency. Reducing bytes alone may not fix that bottleneck.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Why can scaling out compute cause a temporary slowdown?
options: Disaggregation forbids any caching.
All persistent data must always be deleted first.
Adding compute guarantees a slower network by definition.
New compute nodes may have cold caches and trigger additional remote access.
questions.explanation: Cold caches and state/ownership transitions can affect the scale-out period. They must be measured separately from steady state.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A node acknowledges commit before its only log copy reaches durable storage, then loses volatile memory. What may fail?
options: Only the chart colors.
The definition of a vector embedding.
Durability of acknowledged work.
No property, because storage is remote.
questions.explanation: Commit acknowledgment must meet the system’s durable-commit protocol. Remote storage alone does not preserve information never durably recorded.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Does a one-machine delay simulation reproduce a production RDMA/CXL database?
options: No; it can test a narrow model, but hardware and distributed-protocol claims require additional evidence.
No simulation can ever be useful.
Yes, if the simulation uses a GPU.
Yes, whenever the simulated delay matches one measured number.
questions.explanation: A model can isolate a mechanism while omitting bandwidth contention, hardware semantics, failures and control-plane behavior. State that boundary.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question
